fit: firsthand interview priorities in Lewy body dementia
assessment: Telephone interviews of 20 people with dementia with Lewy bodies and 25 caregivers elicited research priorities. The reported experiences and priorities do not estimate a response to dried fig or establish visual episode timing after meals.

fit: Parkinson visual contrast and object identification experiment
assessment: The psychophysical experiment adjusts the contrast of visual stimuli in Parkinson participants with and without hallucinations. Discrimination under the task improves with higher contrast. The outcome is object identification, and it supplies no change in clinical hallucination frequency or fig exposure.

fit: autopsy-confirmed clinical hallucination and delusion profiles
assessment: The retrospective 372-case autopsy cohort compares hallucination and delusion characteristics across confirmed neuropathologies. Presence, content and distress are distinct charted features. The cohort does not relate an identified food exposure to episodes.

fit: Parkinson delusional jealousy and symptom co-occurrence
assessment: The systematic review and small case series describe Parkinson delusional jealousy with medication histories and other symptoms, including visual hallucinations in some records. The primary phenomenon is a delusion, and neither source arm examines dried fig intake.

fit: differential symptom histories in autopsy-defined dementia
assessment: The autopsy study compares clinical and cognitive profiles of LATE neuropathologic change and FTLD-TDP. Visual hallucinations are retrospective symptoms distinguished by pathology. It does not follow a Parkinson culinary intervention.

fit: Parkinson fluctuating pain and visual symptom history
assessment: Records from 331 Parkinson patients are grouped by no pain, nonfluctuating pain and fluctuating pain. The fluctuating-pain group had more people with a visual hallucination history than the no-pain group. This is symptom co-occurrence, without a fig exposure or a change in visual episodes.

fit: Parkinson structural imaging and receptor-map correlations
assessment: The structural imaging synthesis assesses Parkinson visual hallucination groups and compares patterns with independent receptor maps. Regional associations and receptor-map alignment do not provide an intervention, named food exposure or visual episode-rate comparison.

fit: Lewy body symptom-category frequency, duration and connectivity
assessment: The study combines symptom interviews and network imaging in 35 analyzable people with Lewy body disease. It codes hallucination content, duration and frequency separately. Imaging correlations are linked to characteristics of reported phenomena, without a dietary exposure.

fit: clinical hallucination ratings and Lewy body network imaging
assessment: The original compares functional and structural networks across Lewy body dementia hallucination groups. Clinical ratings distinguish degrees of frequency and severity. Imaging and clinical associations do not test eating dried figs.

fit: first Parkinson symptom milestone and survival
assessment: The ParkWest cohort uses predefined clinical thresholds for onset of hallucinations and other disease milestones, then analyzes mortality. Reaching a clinical threshold is distinct from changes in repeated visual episodes. The cohort does not compare dried fig intake.

fit: resting-state network evidence and mixed hallucination definitions
assessment: The review synthesizes resting-state connectivity studies in neurodegenerative conditions with hallucinations. Eleven eligible articles contribute imaging comparisons with heterogeneous symptoms. It does not identify a fig exposure or causal dietary outcome.

fit: visual phenomenology in different psychiatric diagnoses
assessment: This 56-person exploratory study compares visual experience descriptions in schizophrenia, post-traumatic stress disorder and the combination. The measures concern psychiatric groups and trauma-related contexts. No Parkinson fig intake or comparable clinical episode rate is measured.

fit: Parkinson carrier clinical history and cell findings
assessment: The paper combines a Parkinson case associated with an LRRK2 variant and patient-derived cellular comparisons. The original exposure contrast concerns genotype and laboratory function. It does not test dried fig or clinical visual episodes.

fit: postmortem measures and binary Parkinson visual history
assessment: In a small postmortem Parkinson series, six of eight patients had a visual hallucination history. The inspected tissue measures did not show a clear correlation with hallucination presence in the reported regions. The finding is about pathology and a binary history, without dietary exposure.

fit: functional network dynamics by Parkinson hallucination group
assessment: The MRI cohort compares 16 Parkinson visual hallucinators, 75 Parkinson nonhallucinators and 32 controls. Dynamic network states are the outcomes. Classification by clinical report does not establish a dietary cause or measured change in visual episodes.

fit: self-reported visual features and diagnostic limits in an MSA registry
assessment: The Global Multiple System Atrophy Registry survey records patient-reported symptoms, including a proportion who answered that they saw things that were absent. It examines association with levodopa history and discusses diagnostic uncertainty. It does not track fig consumption or episode counts.

fit: optic radiation anatomy by Lewy body visual history
assessment: The MRI comparison evaluates optic radiation features in Lewy body disease grouped by visual hallucination status. Imaging and a clinical history indicator are the relevant measurements. It does not compare dietary exposures.

fit: Parkinson psychosis diagnosis and treatment outcome risks
assessment: The clinical record analysis compares treatment and outcome risks among Parkinson patients with and without psychosis and across medication choices. Hallucinations contribute to the clinical syndrome. Neither the treatment groups nor the measurements identify a fig exposure.

fit: Parkinson pareidolia task and threshold-dependent discrimination
assessment: The 20-item noise task tests whether perceiving nonexistent targets in ambiguous images distinguishes Parkinson participants with a complex hallucination history. Its sensitivity and specificity depend on the task-error threshold. This is a diagnostic task response rather than a dietary effect.

fit: Parkinson imaging review with clinical outcome heterogeneity
assessment: The review systematically compares structural, task-based and resting-state neuroimaging in Parkinson complex and minor hallucinations. Differences in symptom definition and scales are noted. None of the reviewed contrasts measures a specified fig exposure.

fit: Parkinson reasoning task and clinical psychosis association
assessment: A cross-sectional Parkinson comparison tests reasoning with a beads task and assesses psychosis and impulsivity. The reported task performance did not clearly associate with Parkinson psychosis. It does not test an exposure-linked change in visual hallucinations.

fit: pareidolia, visual perception and clinical symptom distinction
assessment: The noise pareidolia task results are interpreted in relation to visuoperceptual performance and reported hallucinations. The findings do not justify treating a laboratory false perception as an equivalent measure of a spontaneous episode. There is no fig exposure.

fit: modeled biomarker and a separate urinary metabolite citation
assessment: Transcriptome-based modeling predicts candidate metabolic changes and cites an earlier urinary salsolinol comparison in levodopa-treated patients. Neither the modeled estimates nor the cited figure establishes fig content or any food-linked clinical visual effect.

fit: reported hallucinations and postmortem nigral loss by sex
assessment: The multicenter clinical-pathological analysis relates substantia nigra cell loss and clinical features by sex. Hallucinations are self- or caregiver-reported clinical features. Tissue loss and symptom history cannot identify a fig-related episode effect.

fit: virtual human estimates and sensed presence rather than visual clinical frequency
assessment: The virtual reality and patient analyses report estimation bias and induced sensed presence. Clinical groups and exclusions distinguish sensed presence from formed visual hallucinations. The test does not identify an oral food exposure or assess episode rate after ingestion.

fit: prodromal diagnostic differential for visual hallucinations
assessment: The pragmatic review distinguishes prodromal Lewy body dementia from prodromal Alzheimer presentations. It emphasizes clinical features including early visual hallucinations and fluctuations. These are diagnostic observations without a fig efficacy comparison.

fit: frontotemporal attention and working-memory profiles
assessment: The frontotemporal dementia study compares attentional, memory and imaging profiles by reported hallucination status and relevant genotype. It distinguishes a visual subgroup. Its disorder, measurements and exposure differ from the frozen Parkinson food premise.

fit: Lewy body visual phenomenology and MRI regional associations
assessment: The MRI comparison includes 28 people with Lewy body disease and visual experiences, separating minor and complex phenomena in ratings. It associates regional structure with symptom characteristics. It contains no food exposure or time-linked change after dried fig.

fit: visual features in atypical parkinsonism diagnostic reassessment
assessment: The retrospective case series describes progressive supranuclear palsy phenotypes in people of South Asian descent. Visual hallucinations prompted consideration of alternative diagnoses in some cases. It supplies no reported fig exposure or diet-linked Parkinson episode rate.

fit: late-life psychosis, visual features and subsequent dementia
assessment: Records of 2,204 people diagnosed with very late-onset psychosis are followed for dementia outcomes. Visual hallucinations and other Lewy body features at onset are predictors. The follow-up outcome is dementia, without a dietary exposure or Parkinson episode-rate contrast.

fit: drug-naïve Parkinson structural MRI comparing visual phenomena
assessment: The study of drug-naïve Parkinson participants compares MRI associations with pareidolia task performance and separately reported visual hallucinations. Distinct imaging patterns are reported. The study contains no dried fig intake or changes in spontaneous episodes after eating.

fit: Parkinson visual hallucination history and urinary biomarker in levodopa users
assessment: The original abstract reports a nearly threefold group difference in mean urinary salsolinol. It compares treated patients with and without visual hallucinations and cites the dried-banana feeding study. The group association identifies a biomarker lead. It supplies no measured fig intake or repeated visual episode rate.

fit: healthy adult dried banana feeding and urinary forms of salsolinol
assessment: Six healthy participants had the urinary S form in both post-intake collection windows. The 24-hour total urinary recovery was reported as 0.75% of the administered amount. Dried banana is a different fruit, and this feeding study does not include Parkinson patients or visual outcome measurements.

fit: banana pulp and peel chemistry by ripeness
assessment: The original banana assay finds salsolinol in later-stage pulp and peel with markedly different table values by preparation. It does not measure Ficus carica or a neurological endpoint. Avoid transferring the measured analyte across fruit species.

fit: banana pulp enzyme and in vitro substrate reaction
assessment: The original abstract measures salsolinol oxidation in banana pulp enzyme assays. It distinguishes a reaction in vitro from diet and clinical outcomes. No dried fig composition or human visual symptom observations are reported.

fit: original 1870 print correspondence showing a mismatched historical citation
assessment: The correspondence cited by the later walnut–fig syrup paper discusses iron and aloes. Two unrelated clinical reports on the same page compare anatomical findings to walnut size. The page does not measure consumption or its reported effect, and it supplies no source for a historical fig or walnut response.
